content: Gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding refers to any bleeding that originates within the gastrointestinal tract. The GI tract is typically divided into two sections: Upper GI bleeding: This involves bleeding from the esophagus (the tube connecting the mouth to the stomach), the stomach, or the first part of the small intestine (duodenum). Lower GI bleeding: This includes bleeding from the remainder of the small intestine, the large intestine (colon), the rectum, or the anus. Symptoms of Gastrointestinal Bleeding The amount of bleeding can vary significantly. In some cases, the bleeding may be so minimal that it is only detectable through laboratory tests, such as a fecal occult blood test. Other symptoms of GI bleeding include: Dark, tarry stools (melena). Passage of large amounts of blood from the rectum. Small amounts of blood visible in the toilet bowl, on toilet paper, or as streaks on stool. Vomiting blood (hematemesis). Massive bleeding from the GI tract can be life-threatening. However, even small amounts of chronic bleeding over time can lead to complications such as anemia or low blood counts. Once the source of bleeding is identified, various treatments are available to stop the bleeding or address the underlying cause. Causes of Gastrointestinal Bleeding GI bleeding can result from conditions that are not necessarily serious, such as: Anal fissures. Hemorrhoids. However, it can also indicate more serious conditions, including cancers of the GI tract, such as: Colon cancer. Small intestine cancer. Stomach cancer. Intestinal polyps (a precancerous condition). Other potential causes include: Abnormal blood vessels in the intestinal lining (angiodysplasias). Bleeding diverticulum or diverticulosis. Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis. Esophageal varices. Esophagitis. Gastric (stomach) ulcers. Intussusception (a condition where the bowel telescopes into itself). Mallory-Weiss tears. Meckel's diverticulum. Radiation injury to the bowel. High-Risk Individuals You should seek medical attention if you experience any of the following: Black, tarry stools (a potential sign of GI bleeding). Blood in your stool. Vomiting blood or material resembling coffee grounds. Diagnosis of Gastrointestinal Bleeding GI bleeding is diagnosed by a physician, and you may or may not be aware of its presence. Home stool tests for microscopic blood may be recommended for individuals with anemia or for colon cancer screening. Your doctor will ask detailed questions about your symptoms, such as: When did you first notice the symptoms? Have you had black, tarry stools or red blood in your stools? Have you vomited blood? Did you vomit material that looked like coffee grounds? Do you have a history of peptic or duodenal ulcers? Have you experienced similar symptoms in the past? Are there any other symptoms you are experiencing? Tests to identify the source of bleeding may include: Abdominal CT scan. Abdominal MRI scan. Abdominal X-ray. Angiography. Bleeding scan (tagged red blood cell scan). Blood clotting tests. Capsule endoscopy (a camera pill swallowed to examine the small intestine). Colonoscopy. Complete blood count (CBC), clotting tests, platelet count, and other laboratory tests. Enteroscopy. Sigmoidoscopy. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care Contact your doctor immediately if you experience: Black, tarry stools. Blood in your stool. Vomiting blood or material resembling coffee grounds. Treatment Options GI bleeding can be a medical emergency requiring immediate attention. Treatment may include: Blood transfusions. Administration of fluids and medications intravenously. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD), a procedure where a thin tube with a camera is passed through the mouth into the esophagus, stomach, and small intestine. Gastric lavage, where a tube is inserted through the mouth into the stomach to drain its contents. Once your condition is stabilized, a thorough physical examination, including a detailed abdominal exam, will be performed. Medications to Avoid Patients diagnosed with GI bleeding should avoid certain medications, such as: Abciximab. Metoclopramide. If you have been diagnosed with GI bleeding, consult your physician before starting or discontinuing any medications. Where to Seek Medical Care If you suspect GI bleeding, seek medical care promptly at a hospital or clinic equipped to handle such conditions.
